articles.title: Mexico charges prosecutor with treason over US involvement in drug raid
articles.summary: The participation of US agents in an April drug operation has raised questions about whether Mexico’s laws were upheld.
articles.body:
Mexico has taken the rare step of charging a former state prosecutor with treason, alleging that he allowed United States agents to take part in a drug raid on the country’s territory.

The case underscores sensitivities about US involvement in Mexico and concerns about the Latin American country’s sovereignty.

On Wednesday, former Chihuahua Attorney General Cesar Jauregui was accused of permitting US agents to take part in an antidrug operation in the northwestern border state.

Under Mexican law, the federal government must approve the activities of foreign forces on the country’s soil.

But questions emerged about whether the law was being adhered to after two US agents and two Mexican law enforcement officials were killed in a car accident on April 19.

News outlets, citing anonymous sources, reported that the US agents had been collaborating with state law enforcement in the destruction of a drug lab.

Matias Gomez Leautaud, an analyst at the Eurasia Group, a US-based risk consultancy firm, told the news service Reuters that the treason charge “seeks to set a precedent and prevent cooperation between [Mexican] states and the US government without the federal government’s coordination and approval”.

While the administration of President Claudia Sheinbaum has collaborated with the US on issues of crime and insecurity, it has opposed any effort by the US to work directly with Mexican states without federal authorisation first.

In the days after the April car crash, Sheinbaum indicated that her government was not aware that US agents had been involved in a drug operation in Chihuahua.

“Evidently, the military didn’t know there were people participating who weren’t Mexican citizens,” Sheinbaum told reporters at the time.

She called for an investigation into whether state officials had respected Mexico’s constitution and its National Security Law, which govern the involvement of foreign forces on Mexican territory.

The constitution, for example, requires Senate approval for the presence of any foreign troops in Mexico. The country has a long history of US intervention , including multiple military invasions continuing into the early 20th century.

But concerns about the US respecting Mexican sovereignty have risen since US President Donald Trump returned to office for a second term.

Trump has suggested that the US could take unilateral military action in Mexico to address cartel drug-trafficking and violence, and he has characterised Mexico’s government as ineffective in addressing the problem.

“We have to eradicate them,” Trump said of the cartels in March. “We have to knock the hell out of them because they’re getting worse. They’re taking over their country. The cartels are running Mexico.”

In the aftermath of the April crash, conflicting reports emerged about why the two US agents were in the country.

Media identified them as members of the Central Intelligence Agency (CIA), a US foreign intelligence branch with a history of covert operations.

But state officials denied claims that they were involved in a drug bust. In a news release on April 20, Jauregui “ruled out the involvement of foreign personnel” in his state’s drug operations.

Instead, he said that US instructors had been present nearby for a training session about drones. They subsequently requested to join a convoy of Mexican law enforcement personnel to return to the airport, according to Jauregui.

“It is worth explaining what happened, in order to clarify the facts that are causing some confusion,” Jauregui said at the time.

He resigned from his post as state attorney general later that month.

Mexico’s federal Attorney General Ernestina Godoy has since accused Jauregui of permitting foreign agents to participate in operations on Mexican territory without first sharing information with federal officials.

A judge has ordered Jauregui to be held in pretrial detention as the court decides whether there is sufficient evidence to move forward with a criminal case.

Experts say the treason charge he faces is vaguely defined in Mexican law. It broadly covers acts that undermine Mexico’s sovereignty for the benefit of a foreign entity.

Convictions are rare, with the last widely recognised example coming in 1867, when Emperor Maximilian was tried by court-martial and subsequently executed for crimes against Mexico.

Jauregui is a member of the National Action Party, a conservative political movement in Mexico. Sheinbaum, meanwhile, is a leader in the left-wing Morena party.

articles.title: Subtropical Storm Josephine forms off Mid-Atlantic coast
articles.summary: The storm doesn’t have much to offer, but parts of the coast will experience wind and flooding.
articles.body: Subtropical Storm Josephine just formed off the coast of the Mid-Atlantic, but will largely be nothing more than a nuisance for coastal areas as it moves north. The storm is 265 miles south of Nantucket and has nearly 65 mph sustained winds, according to the National Hurricane Center. Josephine is the 10th named storm of the 2026 Atlantic hurricane season, which continues to run well behind schedule. The 10th named storm typically forms in late September, but a powerful El Niño has helped suppress storm activity in the Atlantic this season. Josephine is expected to remain well off the East Coast while tracking northeast Thursday before dissipating this weekend. Subtropical storms share some characteristics with tropical systems, including drawing energy from warm ocean water, but also have features of non-tropical storms like nor’easters. The distinction makes little difference when it comes to impacts: Subtropical storms can still bring strong winds, heavy rain and coastal flooding. Some strengthening is expected over the next 36 hours, with hurricane-force winds by late Thursday as Josephine becomes a post-tropical storm. Fortunately, most of Josephine’s wind and rain are expected to remain over the open Atlantic. Breezy to windy conditions will continue to impact parts of the East Coast through Thursday, particularly Cape Cod, Massachusetts. Coastal flooding is also possible around high tide from the Mid-Atlantic to Cape Cod through Friday. With most of the rain staying offshore, much of the East Coast is expected to remain dry through the end of the week and into the weekend. Some wind-driven rain could reach Cape Cod Wednesday night into Thursday morning.

articles.title: Rosatom completes supply of engineered safety features actuation systems for Kudankulam N-plant units 3 and 4
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Russia state atomic energy corporation Rosatom’s division Rosatom Automated Control Systems has completed the supply of equipment for
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Russia state atomic energy corporation Rosatom’s division Rosatom Automated Control Systems has completed the supply of equipment for engineered safety features actuation system computerised subsystems (ESFAS CS) for units 3 and 4 of the Kudankulam nuclear power plant in Tamil Nadu. The role of the general designer and supplier of equipment in the project belongs to Atomstroyexport.In total, about 300 items of equipment were manufactured and delivered to the plant – four sets of ESFAS CS in accordance with the number of safety instrumentation and control trains, per each power unit featuring VVER-1000 reactors.ESFAS is the system that monitors the process parameters of a power unit when there is a deviation from normal operation conditions. In case of an accident, the system automatically initiates the start of safety instrumentation and control systems and sends commands to actuators (boron injection pumps and other active protection means) in order to prevent a beyond-design-basis accident and bring the reactor plant to a safe state. The system also ensures reactor cooldown, which is a controlled decrease of coolant temperature and pressure down to safe values after the shutdown.To avoid simultaneous failure, they are physically separated — located in different rooms — and have autonomous power supply from separate diesel generators.Specialists developing the ESFAS CS for units 3 and 4 relied on the operating experience of the same system at Kudankulam NPP units 1 and 2, which allowed them to implement a number of optimised solutions. One of such solutions is the application of non-programmable modules that process signals from sensors without the use of microprocessors. This helps to reduce the dependence of safety functions on application software and increases the resistance of equipment to potential common cause failures.The final delivery of ESFAS CS equipment was yet another step of equipping the power units with Russian automation, control and safety systems, implemented through industrial cooperation. Installation on the site will be followed by the pre-commissioning stage, which includes the off-line and integrated tests of the systems. Following the tests, the systems will be prepared for commissioning and further operation at units 3 and 4 of the Kudankulam plant.Kudankulam plant features six power units with VVER-1000 reactors, with the total installed capacity of 6,000 MW. The first phase (units 1 and 2) was commissioned in 2013 and 2017, respectively. The second phase (Units 3 and 4) is under construction.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.summary: YouTube star MrBeast, whose real name is Jimmy Donaldson, is helping expand access to healthcare in underserved communities by supporting the
articles.body: YouTube star MrBeast, whose real name is Jimmy Donaldson, is helping expand access to healthcare in underserved communities by supporting the establishment of five medical clinics across the United States and abroad. In a video posted on Beast Philanthropy in April 2026, the content creator showcased the initiative undertaken with his team and nonprofit organisation BUILD to bring essential medical services closer to people who struggle to access them.The five clinics are located in the US, Nigeria, Ukraine and Kenya, with each facility designed to address a specific healthcare challenge. Built using shipping containers, the clinics aim to provide medical assistance in areas where healthcare infrastructure is limited, emergency services are difficult to access or specialised treatment remains out of reach for many families.MrBeast helps establish first medical clinic in a remote Texas communityOne of the clinics has been established in Chester, Texas, where residents have faced difficulties accessing emergency medical assistance. According to the video, two medical emergencies occurred at a local school during the year, with ambulances taking almost an hour to arrive.The new facility, described in the video as the first medical clinic in Chester, includes a telehealth centre where residents can consult doctors and seek guidance about their health concerns. The clinic will be run by Timber, a local resident who grew up in the community and expressed a desire to help the people living there.The facility is expected to give residents a more accessible point of contact for medical assistance, particularly in a community where reaching healthcare providers can be challenging.Nigeria clinic aims to help children access heart surgeryAnother clinic has been sent to a hospital in Nigeria to help children access screening for open-heart surgery. The video highlights the difficulties families face in obtaining specialised cardiac treatment, particularly when the cost of travelling abroad for surgery becomes a major financial burden.One person featured in the video said that the procedure could cost between $50,000 and $117,000 in the United States. The new facility is intended to help doctors screen more patients and improve access to potential treatment opportunities.According to the video, the clinic could serve an additional 2,000 people in the community over the course of a year, expanding the hospital's ability to identify patients who need specialised care.Medical clinic deployed to Ukraine amid ongoing warA third clinic has been deployed to communities near the front lines of the war in Ukraine, where the conflict has damaged hospitals and disrupted access to essential healthcare services.The initiative was carried out in collaboration with the Daar Foundation, with the aim of ensuring that local doctors have the supplies needed to assist residents. The video also states that BUILD has four other active clinics across the war zone.The new facility is intended to support communities dealing with the consequences of the conflict, where damaged infrastructure and disrupted medical services have made access to healthcare increasingly difficult.Kenya clinic to expand clubfoot treatment for childrenIn Kenya, another clinic will help children born with clubfoot, a condition that can affect their ability to walk if left untreated. The facility is being established in a coastal community in Kilifi County, where families in rural areas can struggle to access specialised treatment.The project works with Hope Walks, an organisation that has been serving children in the area for 14 years. Before the new facility, the team had been treating patients from a single small room, limiting the number of children it could help each week.Clubfoot can often be treated without surgery through a process in which doctors gradually reposition the foot using a series of casts. The new clinic is expected to expand the organisation's capacity and enable it to treat more children.The initiative also highlights the importance of early intervention, particularly in communities where children with disabilities and their families may face social stigma alongside the challenges of obtaining medical care.Fifth clinic in Massachusetts to offer free health screeningsThe fifth clinic has been sent to a housing village in Worcester, Massachusetts. It will provide free health, vision and dental screenings to residents, including children and grandparents.According to the April 2026 video, the facility is expected to serve more than 40 families every week, allowing residents to access essential screenings without having to pay for them.The clinic is part of the broader effort to make basic healthcare services more accessible to people who might otherwise struggle to obtain preventive care.BUILD's healthcare initiatives aim to reach thousandsThe Beast Philanthropy video explains that BUILD began in 2013 as a student-led initiative and has since deployed 60 clinics across 24 countries, impacting more than 200,000 people.Across the five clinics featured in the video, the team estimates that more than 10,000 people a year will be impacted. The video also states that over 2,500 people had already been reached by the time filming took place, with another 10,000 expected to benefit over the following year.The initiative has also received support from Neuro Gum. According to the video, the company created limited-edition tins, with proceeds going towards projects aimed at helping communities.By addressing different healthcare needs, from emergency access in rural Texas and cardiac screening in Nigeria to medical assistance in Ukraine, clubfoot treatment in Kenya and free screenings in Massachusetts, the project seeks to bring essential services closer to underserved populations.You use AI every day. articles.title: Firefighters 'knowingly put at risk' during summer wildfires
articles.summary: Crews and control centre staff say the fires were relentless with many firefighters still off work injured.
articles.body:
Firefighters and the public were knowingly put at risk during this year's wildfires due to chronic underfunding, a union has said.

Those working on the ground and in the South Wales control centre said the fires were relentless with injuries "commonplace" for crews.

The Fire Brigades Union (FBU) said firefighters were climbing hills in unsuitable boots and non-breathable layers used for house fires due to not having enough kit, and there is a "real risk to the public" if immediate action isn't taken.

The Welsh government said it doesn't provide the core funding but "recognise the concerns raised and are clear that we need to do all we can to reduce the risk of wildfires".

Sean Cayford, a firefighter in Bridgend, said crews were told in mid August that there were no pumps or fire appliances available across the brigade's entire region.

"I've never heard that before but that was heard again later in the wildfire season. That was startling," he said.

"One particular day we were at an incident on top of Tredegar mountain and as we looked around the landscape we could see in the region of six or seven other category three wildfires, the most serious type of wildfires, on the horizon in every direction you looked."

Sean said even with help from other brigades from all over the UK, they "still didn't have enough" firefighters.

"We were stretched so thinly," he said. "It has an increasingly destructive affect on the morale of our firefighters.

"It's very difficult to be at a wildfire incident in excess for eight or 10 or 12 hours and not get injured to some degree."

He said colleagues sustained lower limb injuries and heat illness, with many still unable to work.

Gemma Thomas, who works in the control centre, said the average number of calls is usually 200-300 but on their busiest day this summer they had almost 2,000.

"It was just relentless in there," she said.

"There were times where we were unable to fulfil the requests that were coming from the incidents.

"We are the first point of contact for somebody who is having potentially the worst day of their life.

"It was so stressful, mentally draining, that you're getting home from work absolutely shattered to think right I've got to back and do it all again tomorrow."

Gemma said there were times when staff needed to take breaks "one at a time for 10 minutes just to get people out of the room".

"People were getting to the point where they were just shattered in work, shattered at home," she said, adding there was no work-life balance because they needed to use free time to rest.

Gemma says the support from management within the team was "phenomenal" and "even the firefighters on the ground were understanding how stretched we were in the control room".

But she doesn't believe they could sustain it long term and wants to see an increase in numbers of firefighters.

First Minister Rhun ap Iorwerth is hosting a climate change and resilience summit in Merthyr Tydfil on Thursday, which will "bring key partners together to develop future actions".

It will host representatives from the fire services and police, local government, farmers and climate change organisations.

"There was poor preparation," said Gareth Tovey, executive council member for Wales, explaining they redirected specialist crews such as water teams to the wildfires.

"At some stages there was zero crew back up for vast parts of south Wales," he said.

"Firefighters were injured because they didn't have the right kit to fight wildfires."

The FBU says there's a shortfall of 400 firefighters in Wales.

Tovey said the union had been warning "for years" that authorities needed to do something and there was a "real risk to the public" if immediate action isn't taken.

Tovey said bringing in the army , while helpful, "is not a silver bullet" as they do not have the firefighting skills needed.

An FBU survey following the fires found 69% of firefighters felt significantly under-equipped, with just 8% feeling fully equipped.

Nearly half reported welfare facilities during wildfire deployment were insufficient.

Firefighters are funded by the public but through a levy decided by the local authority for the area. This is part of their budget, which is in turn set by the Welsh government.

North Wales Fire and Rescue Service is applying to the Welsh government's emergency assistance scheme to cover the additional £500,000 the wildfires this summer cost.

At one point firefighters in north Wales were managing six wildfires at once - more than ever before.

It comes as a new report from the UK's Environment, Food and Rural Affairs Committee said the wildfires left firefighters working in extreme conditions and exposed weaknesses in the UK's resilience and preparation.

They called for a UK government-funded "national wildfire prevention campaign" with clear and consistent messaging, along with wildfire risk indicators in weather forecasts.

The Welsh government said individual fire and rescue authorities determine how many firefighters they need and set their budgets accordingly.

"They should take this summer's wildfires into account when doing so," a spokesperson said.

Ahead of the summit, ap Iorwerth said: "What we saw this summer was much more dangerous than fires in other years.

"While we cannot reverse climate change, we can take practical steps to keep the risk of wildfire as low as possible and ensure a swift and effective response to incidents."

South Wales Fire and Rescue Service said: "We are incredibly proud of the professionalism, resilience and commitment shown by our firefighters, control colleagues and everyone who supported the response, often in extremely challenging conditions."

"We recognise that the changing climate and evolving risks facing fire and rescue services mean we must continue to learn, adapt and strengthen our ability to respond when demand rises sharply."

It said it was engaging with unions about the investment needed and would be a key voice at the summit.

Mid and West Wales Fire and Rescue Service's chief fire officer Craig Flanney added climate-related emergencies are having a real impact on communities, environment and public services, and require a collective effort.

articles.title: Emma Thompson and Greg Wise welcomed a Rwandan refugee into their family after a Christmas charity meeting; he had escaped a rebel camp and prison before rebuilding his life in Britain
articles.summary: For Tindyebwa Agaba, arriving in Britain did not immediately mean finding safety.
articles.body: For Tindyebwa Agaba, arriving in Britain did not immediately mean finding safety. He had lost contact with his sisters, spent years under the control of armed rebels in Central Africa and escaped prison before reaching the UK as an asylum seeker. At one point, he was sleeping rough in central London. A chance meeting at a Christmas gathering organised for refugees brought him into the lives of actors Emma Thompson and Greg Wise, who gradually welcomed him into their family. The relationship gave Agaba a connection he had not expected to find. In the years that followed, he pursued higher education and work focused on human rights, protection and criminal investigation.How poverty, conflict and displacement changed Agaba’s childhoodAgaba grew up in Rwanda in a family that had little money but managed to send its children to school. His father worked as a farmer, and his mother cared for the family. That arrangement changed when his father died of Aids while Agaba was nine. Without his income, the children could no longer continue their education as before.His mother took Agaba and his sisters across the border into Uganda, where she persuaded Care International to help them with accommodation and schooling. The arrangement offered the children a degree of stability, but it did not last. As violence spread across the region during the 1990s, aid organisations began withdrawing from areas where their staff could no longer work safely.Agaba and his sisters eventually returned to their home village in Rwanda. Still children, they found themselves living in a largely abandoned family house while armed groups operated nearby. When Agaba was about 12, armed men seized him, his sisters and other children. They were taken across the border into the Democratic Republic of Congo after several days travelling through unfamiliar terrain. During the journey, the children were separated by gender. His sisters went with the girls, and he never saw them again.How Agaba escaped armed rebels before fleeing to UgandaAgaba spent approximately two and a half years at a rebel camp. The boys were expected to carry out a range of duties, including gathering food, keeping watch and investigating activity in the surrounding area. Some assignments involved risks that children could scarcely understand or avoid. Agaba later spoke about the experience with caution, making clear that certain memories remained difficult to discuss.Escape required patience as much as opportunity. He and a small group of friends spent months considering how they might get away without being caught. They eventually decided to act during a night watch, when they believed they had a better chance of leaving without attracting immediate attention.The attempt came at a cost. Agaba managed to escape, but one of his friends was shot. The boys found work herding cattle in another part of the country before eventually returning to their former village. By then, they had been associated with rebel forces fighting the government. Local police arrested them, apparently treating their involvement as voluntary rather than recognising the circumstances in which they had been recruited.Agaba spent about eight months in prison before escaping following a confrontation with a guard. He crossed into Uganda, where a Care International worker recognised him and helped arrange his onward journey. He was eventually brought to London, where he sought asylum.How a Refugee Council Christmas event brought Agaba and Emma Thompson togetherReaching Britain did not bring an immediate end to his difficulties. Agaba struggled to secure the support he needed and, in November 2003, found himself sleeping outdoors in Trafalgar Square. His circumstances began to change after he encountered the Refugee Council, which helped him find accommodation and invited him to one of its Christmas events for refugees.It was there that he met Thompson. At the time, he had little reason to recognise her as a famous actor. She was attending the gathering as a supporter of the charity, where she sometimes helped prepare or serve food to people seeking refuge in the UK.Thompson offered Agaba a lift to north London, where he was staying, and the contact developed from there. She and her husband, actor Greg Wise, later invited him to spend Christmas with them and their young daughter, Gaia. Over time, he became a familiar presence in their household, moving beyond the circumstances of their first meeting.Agaba did not initially realise that the woman who had offered him help was one of Britain's best-known actors. He discovered her identity months later at college, when a film adaptation of Shakespeare's Henry V was shown in class. Seeing Thompson on screen, he told his teacher that he had spent time with her the previous weekend. The teacher apparently assumed he was joking.The connection with Thompson and Wise was not presented as a formal adoption. Rather, Agaba became part of their family life, building a relationship with the couple that continued after the initial Christmas invitation. His experience in London had begun with uncertainty about where he would sleep.Education and work with vulnerable communitiesAgaba went on to study politics and complete a master's degree. He later worked with the United Nations High Commissioner for Human Rights, including on issues affecting refugees and asylum seekers arriving in Cairo from other parts of Africa. His professional work took him to several countries, among them Liberia, South Sudan, Palestine and Myanmar.The work brought him into contact with people whose lives had been shaped by conflict, displacement and involvement with armed groups. Agaba said his own background sometimes helped him establish trust with former combatants. He worked on protection issues through different organisations, including international agencies and charities. Rather than remaining permanently in one location, he took on assignments in different parts of the world.His later career also extended into criminal investigation, building on his experience of protection work and the circumstances in which vulnerable people become caught up in violence and crime. The professional direction reflected a continuing interest in the people affected by conflict, including those whose experiences are often poorly understood by the authorities they encounter.How Agaba turned childhood trauma into a career helping refugeesAgaba's relationship with Thompson and Wise remained a significant part of his story, but it was only one element of the life he built after arriving in Britain. His education and international work took him far beyond London, while his experiences as a child gave him a perspective that informed his dealings with refugees and former combatants.His early years had been marked by separation, forced recruitment and the loss of contact with his sisters. In Britain, a meeting at a charity event led to a lasting family connection at a time when he was struggling to establish himself. From there, Agaba pursued qualifications and work that brought him into contact with people facing some of the same kinds of insecurity he had known as a child.You use AI every day. articles.title: Arizona mom whose son was found alive in hospital morgue speaks out: ‘It’s an unexplainable feeling’
articles.summary: Alexus Fiordilino said she thought her 18-month-old son, Vincent, was still breathing when she gave him a final hug, but the emergency room doctor insisted he was gone.
articles.body: The mother of a toddler found alive in an Arizona hospital morgue in February more than five hours after he was pronounced dead said Wednesday she thought she heard him breathing when she hugged him goodbye. But instead of listening to her gut, Alexus Fiordilino said, she believed the doctor who told her those were 18-month-old Vincent’s last gasps and that any further attempts to save him would just prolong his agony. “As a mom you don’t want to hear that,” Fiordilino, 30, said in an interview. “I didn’t want him to suffer. It seemed to be they’d done everything they could. And then he called it.” Fiordilino was referring to Dr. Aryan Toosi, who pronounced Vincent dead at 6:20 p.m. on Super Bowl Sunday at Mercy Gilbert Medical Center in Gilbert, Arizona. A little over five hours later, Fiordilino said, police were questioning her and her husband, Angelo, when a detective burst into the room and told them that a medical examiner’s employee who had come to collect Vincent’s body had discovered he was still alive. “My husband and I just screamed in relief,” she said. “We were praising the Lord. We were crying. To go from hearing he was gone and then finding out he isn’t gone, it’s an unexplainable feeling.” Fiordilino spoke out more than eight months after her son’s remarkable story of survival after he nearly drowned in the family swimming pool made national headlines and sparked multiple investigations into what happened on Feb. 8. The Gilbert Police Department had recommended filing child abuse charges against both parents for losing track of Vincent while a Super Bowl party was going on at their residence. “Both admitted to smoking marijuana the morning of the drowning,” the police report said. But Maricopa County Attorney Rachel Mitchell announced in July that the Fiordilinos would not be charged. Fiordilino’s lawyer, John Brewer, said he plans to file a formal complaint this week against Toosi and the hospital. He said a review of Vincent’s medical records shows that critical test results that Toosi cited to justify ending efforts to save the child were not completed until after the toddler was declared dead. “The parents were faced with having to decide whether to keep trying to revive their son, and the doctor provided them with false information,” Brewer said. “That’s beyond a conscious disregard for human life.” Brewer’s office turned its records over to the Gilbert Police Department, which said it forwarded everything to the state attorney general’s office for review. The AG’s office said Wednesday that it has not made a decision to review this case. Toosi’s lawyer, Scott Holden, released a statement in response. “Dr. Toosi’s thoughts are with the young patient and family, and he wishes the child continued healing and recovery,” it said. “His commitment to delivering high-quality care has always been rooted in a desire to provide healing, safety and comfort to his community.” Meanwhile, the hospital called the situation “heartbreaking” in a statement. “Out of respect for the patient’s privacy, we cannot share any information and we are unable to comment on those involved in patient care,” it said. “Patient safety and exceptional care are our highest priorities.” Asked how Vincent is doing now, Fiordilino said, “He’s getting better.” Brewer said that while the boy is home with his family, he has many health challenges. “Vincent is severely brain-injured,” he said. “He can’t swallow. He seizes up. He can’t sit up on his own or crawl.” The tragic turn of events began around 5:38 p.m. Feb. 8 with a 911 call for help after Vincent was found floating face down in the family pool and a relative tried to revive him by performing CPR, according to a police report obtained by NBC affiliate KPNX of Phoenix. Vincent was rushed to the emergency room at Mercy Gilbert Medical Center, where an ER team that included Toosi took over the effort to save him. At 6:13 p.m., according to the report, Toosi went out to deliver bad news to the boy’s parents. “As long as there are no objections, I’d like to call time of death,” Toosi said, according to the report. Then, “at approximately 18:20 hours, Dr. Toosi called the time of death and requested a moment of silence.” Just as Fiordilino told NBC News, police officers who had been in the ER said in the report that the child still appeared to be gasping for breath after he was declared dead. A detective reported then hearing “another audible gasp” at around 7:18 p.m. as the ER workers were preparing to move Vincent from the trauma room to the “cold room” that serves as the hospital’s morgue and where the temperature is set at 36 to 39 degrees. The same detective said that when he returned to photograph the body an hour later, he “again observed what appeared to be a gasp or air release.” “The nurse again stated it was agonal breathing and explained it was due to compressions, oxygen, and possible pressure applied by family members while saying goodbye,” the report says. And at 7:23 p.m., “the cold room door was closed,” the report says. More than four hours later, when the medical examiner’s team arrived at 11:52 p.m. to retrieve the boy, “he was found breathing,” the report says. “The family was notified immediately,” and the boy was airlifted to Phoenix Children’s Hospital. Fiordilino said that when she saw her son again in the pediatric intensive care unit, “he was hooked up to all kinds of monitors and things.” “He looked like a different baby,” she said. “It’s something I hope no other parent has to live through.”

articles.title: Canadian publisher drops writer Thelyson Orelien over AI use in novel
articles.summary: Publisher Boreal says investigations confirmed the Haitian-Canadian Thelyson Orelien used AI in his breakthrough novel.
articles.body:
The publisher of best-selling Haitian-Canadian writer Thelyson Orelien says it has severed its professional relationship with the author after confirming he used artificial intelligence to help write his novel, “It Was Either That or Die”.

Boreal said on Wednesday that it conducted a further investigation after allegations surfaced in September to determine whether AI was used to write the novel.

“New information, confirmed over the past few days, indicates that artificial intelligence was used in the writing process” of the novel, a Boreal statement said.

Orelien had previously denied allegations surrounding his breakthrough novel, and last week, the Canadian publisher said it was standing by the 38-year-old writer.

Boreal said it did not know the extent of AI’s use in the writing process “and we will likely never have a definitive answer”.

It said it gathered all the working versions of the novel and hired an outside party to analyse the various drafts.

“The results obtained this week revealed traces of AI tags in the metadata of certain documents,” Boreal said.

The publisher said it had tried to work with Orelien to gather the evidence necessary to prove his innocence.

That effort was inconclusive, and Orelien “subsequently announced that he would not provide any further information,” the publisher said.

Orelien’s novel about migration, known by its original French title “C’etait ca ou mourir”, had been scheduled for translation in more than 20 countries.

France’s top book prize, the Goncourt, removed “C’etait ca ou mourir” from its shortlist after tests with the AI detector Pangram indicated a 100 percent probability that it contained computer-generated text.

But Orelien called the allegations “slander and heresy” in a statement sent to AFP earlier this month.

“Here and there I did use tools for research, particularly for foreign idioms,” he said.

“But not a single sentence in this book was created by a machine, nor the meaning or the structure of a story that comes from my gut,” Orelien said.

On Wednesday, he stood firm, telling the French newspaper Liberation that he had used AI “in the creative process” for “historical research”.

The author said he began writing the book in late 2017, before AI services such as ChatGPT were widely available.

When the allegations first surfaced in September, Orelien said he suspected racism was behind the attacks on him.

articles.title: Making whiskey at home could land you in prison, but Supreme Court may change that
articles.summary: The Supreme Court will review an 1868 federal law that makes home distilling a felony, a case that could redefine congressional taxing power.
articles.body: Americans can legally brew beer and make wine at home, but producing even a small amount of whiskey could land them in federal prison. Now, the U.S. Supreme Court is preparing to weigh in on a 150-year-old federal law prohibiting home distilling, a case that could have implications far beyond the liquor cabinet. The justices agreed Monday to review the Reconstruction-era restriction, which dates to 1868 and was originally enacted to combat liquor tax evasion. AMERICANS ONCE SURVIVED ON SQUIRREL PIE, WHISKEY AND HOMEMADE CHEESE AFTER BRITISH IMPORTS DRIED UP Robert Alt, president and CEO of the Ohio-based Buckeye Institute, which represents challengers to the ban, told Fox News Digital the decision marks a significant development for home-distilling enthusiasts. "This is a real opportunity for both whiskey and freedom," Alt said. Among those challenging the prohibition is John Ream, an Ohio brewery owner and former aerospace engineer who wants to distill small quantities of spirits at home for personal consumption. Ream's legal battle was previously highlighted by Fox News Digital as he awaited word on whether the nation's highest court would intervene. MAN CHALLENGING 150-YEAR-OLD BAN ON MAKING LIQUOR AT HOME HOPES SUPREME COURT TAKES HIS CASE Under federal law, producing distilled spirits at home can carry penalties of up to five years in prison, a $10,000 fine and possible property forfeiture. The case centers on whether Congress' constitutional authority to collect taxes also allows it to prohibit an otherwise lawful activity inside a person's home. "What this case boils down to is what is the scope of congressional power?" Alt said. Two federal appeals courts reached conflicting conclusions earlier this year. CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER The 5th Circuit struck down the restriction, finding that Congress' taxing authority did not justify the prohibition. The 6th Circuit upheld the law, concluding it was a permissible means of enforcing federal liquor taxes. The Department of Justice (DOJ) maintains that the restriction is a legitimate tool for preventing tax evasion and protecting federal revenue. The DOJ declined to comment on the case to Fox News Digital. "The founders would be rolling over in their graves at the suggestion that Congress had the authority to ban and make a felony out of this very American activity." Alt, however, argues that allowing Congress to prohibit home distilling under its taxing authority could establish a troubling precedent for other private activities. He pointed to hobbies such as gardening and working on cars as examples of activities that could theoretically face similar restrictions under the government's legal reasoning. The attorney also noted that home distilling has deep American roots. President George Washington participated in home distilling, Alt said. A ruling favoring the federal government would leave the challenged restriction in place, although Congress could still amend the law, Alt said. articles.title: New Mexico sues Epstein lawyer and accountant, accusing them of hiding his crimes
articles.summary: Both men have denied having any knowledge of Epstein's crimes and their attorney rejected the lawsuit as "categorically false".
articles.body:
Prosecutors in the US state of New Mexico have filed a civil lawsuit against two longtime aides of Jeffrey Epstein, accusing the men of profiting from the late financier's sex trafficking ring.

Lawyer Darren Indyke and accountant Richard Kahn are the sole executors of Epstein's estate, controlling all his wealth and possessions. They have denied any role in his crimes.

New Mexico Attorney General Raúl Torrez says they played a key role in concealing abuse at Epstein's remote Zorro Ranch near the city of Santa Fe, and that they continue to earn money while victims seek accountability.

The lawsuit is separate to the state's ongoing criminal probe into Epstein, which was re-launched in February.

An attorney representing both Indyke and Kahn told the BBC that they "emphatically reject" the claims in the lawsuit.

The lawsuit was filed in New Mexico on Wednesday under the federal Trafficking Victims Protection Act and New Mexico Racketeering Act.

During a news conference, Torrez argued that the two men are blocking efforts by Epstein's victims to seek compensation from his fortune, estimated at roughly $635m (£474m) at the time of his death.

"Those resources rightfully belong in the hands of survivors - there should be no distribution of Mr Epstein's remaining assets to people like Mr Indyke and Mr Kahn for participation in what I think is one of the most horrific criminal enterprises in modern America," he said.

Both men worked with Epstein for decades, and have previously testified to Congress that they were unaware of the crimes he committed alongside accomplice Ghislane Maxwell.

Their attorney Daniel Weiner said in a statement to the BBC that, "they are confident that they will prevail on the claims asserted against them".

"Both Mr Indyke and Mr Kahn reject as categorically false the allegations that they knowingly facilitated or assisted Mr Epstein in his sexual abuse or trafficking of women, or that they were aware of Mr Epstein's actions while they provided legal or accounting services to him," Weiner said.

He added that the New Mexico prosecutor never asked to speak to either man "before filing this baseless lawsuit", and that they both have "cooperated with any and all investigations when asked to do so".

Jeffrey Epstein had two key aides - why do they still control his money and secrets?

Epstein tried to buy a palace in Morocco days before his arrest in 2019

The two aides were named as co-executors in August 2019 by Epstein, just two days before he killed himself in jail while awaiting trial on child sex-trafficking charges.

He revised his will to transfer all his wealth into a trust named after the year of his birth, which the lawyer and accountant would administer.

In their role as executors, Indyke and Kahn agreed to fund compensation packages for survivors that included conditions that prevented survivors who accepted funds from taking further legal action against them personally. Other claims are still outstanding.

As beneficiaries of the trust, the men could also be paid tens of millions of dollars each from whatever remains when the claims are settled.

In his remarks, Torrez alleged that Epstein's crimes were "made possible by handlers, by lawyers, by accountants, by others who have yet to face real consequence".

"Jeffrey Epstein did not operate alone, and his death does not end the pursuit of accountability for the people who helped make his crimes possible," he said.

"Those who allegedly enabled this exploitation should not be allowed to profit from it while survivors continue to live with its consequences," he added.

articles.title: Hetland Hall Hotel expansion set for approval despite stables' horse fall fears
articles.summary: A nearby stables opposes plans to expand the Hetland Hall Hotel, creating up to 60 jobs.
articles.body:
Plans to expand a country house hotel in southern Scotland have been recommended for approval despite fears they could increase risks for horse riders at a neighbouring stable.

The RAD Hotel Group wants to extend its Hetland Hall Hotel near Carrutherstown, creating up to 60 jobs.

Hetland Hill Stables - where a young rider died after a fall in 2019 - has objected due to concerns that visitors to the proposed lodges might bring dogs which could spook its horses.

However, a report to Dumfries and Galloway Council (DGC) said the closest lodge would be about 30ft (9m) from the boundary and that was considered to be "appropriate" separation from the gallops.

Country house hotel expansion could deliver 60 jobs

Rider's fatal horse fall 'unforeseeable'

The hotel plans, lodged earlier this year, include 26 extra bedrooms, a spa and wellness facility and the creation of a new wedding and events space along with 10 woodland lodges.

The company said that if they were approved the proposals would "significantly enhance the hotel's wedding, accommodation and leisure offering".

DGC's planning committee is being recommended to approve them.

However, a submission on behalf of Hetland Hill Stables warned that the density of the proposed lodges near its gallops created "severe safety risks".

"Thoroughbred race horses are highly strung and the proposed residential and leisure areas pose a unique threat to the horses, the public and the riders," it said.

"If one of the horses is spooked by the slightest noise this can result in the horse and rider falling and bringing down others and this has happened in the past which resulted in a fatal outcome."

Natasha Galpin, 22, died after falling off her horse at the stables in January 2019.

A fatal accident inquiry later concluded it had been a "tragic, immediate, unforeseen and unforeseeable accident".

The council report on the hotel expansion noted the objection by the stables but concluded steps had been taken to address their concerns.

It said planting had been carried out to fill a gap in the trees in the area and also that the lodges had been positioned to face the hotel rather than the gallops.

It has recommended approval for the plans with a condition attached that any lodges should be removed within two months if they become "redundant or obsolete for any reason".

articles.title: In 2025, a relative of Subway co-founder Peter Buck bought a Connecticut warehouse held by another family for three generations for $6.75 million; now a $1.8 million renovation and 10,000-square-foot office are planned
articles.summary: A relative of the late Subway co-founder and philanthropist Peter Buck has bought a prominent Danbury warehouse that had remained in another local family
articles.body: A relative of the late Subway co-founder and philanthropist Peter Buck has bought a prominent Danbury warehouse that had remained in another local family for three generations. The buyer, using the company name Swampfield LLC, purchased the former Dandy Foods property on Mill Plain Road for $6.75 million in March 2025 and plans to invest another $1.8 million in renovations. The project includes a new 10,000-square-foot office building, according to Hearst Connecticut Media’s News-Times and New Haven Register. Read more details about it,as per the reports,here:A property changes handsThe 4.8-acre warehouse site was developed by entrepreneur Albert Salame and remained in his family for three generations. After Salame’s death in 2023, his family began selling parts of his local real estate portfolio, including the Dandy Foods property. Swampfield LLC completed the purchase in March 2025. The company is connected to a private member of the Buck family, whose philanthropic and land conservation investments are managed through PCW Management Center in Mystic.Ben Benoit, president of PCW Management Center, said in the reports that the long-term plan is for the building to remain a warehouse. He added that the renovation will also create offices for a private Buck family member and a property management office that he runs.What the renovation will includeThe existing warehouse needs substantial work, and the new owners plan to bring it back into good condition. While no tenants have been announced for the larger warehouse space, the family intends to keep the site in productive use rather than redevelop it into something entirely different.Danbury’s planning and zoning department has approved blueprints for a 10,000-square-foot office building attached to the west side of the warehouse. The new offices are intended to support the Buck family’s charities, land holdings and related enterprises.The approved site improvements include additional landscaping, a concrete sidewalk along Mill Plain Road and the formalisation of parking areas. The city made one condition for approval: the new owner must remove six empty semi-trailers parked on the front lawn of the warehouse.A continuing Buck family legacyPeter Buck co-founded Subway in 1965 with Fred DeLuca and became one of Danbury’s most significant philanthropists before his death in 2021. The warehouse purchase is being viewed as a continuation of that legacy of investment in the city.Benoit said, as per the reports, that he knew Albert Salame and that the purchase made sense after Salame’s death, when his family was ready to retire from the property. He described the building as needing work and said the family is focused on restoring it. The deal is also part of a wider transition in Salame’s former real estate holdings. In 2025, the Salame family sold the nearby Maron Hotel for $5 million and later sold the adjacent building housing Stop & Shop for $16 million.Why Mill Plain Road mattersThe warehouse is located next to Agriventures Agway and a strip of retail and commercial businesses along Mill Plain Road, a corridor that carries an average of 14,000 drivers each day. Its location offers strong visibility and convenient access for future commercial activity.The renovation is the latest investment in an area that has been attracting attention. City leaders have confirmed serious discussions about converting the former Super 8 motel at 3 Lake Ave Extension into senior housing, while a Ridgefield businessman has said two tenants are expected at the former Puppy Love site at 37 Lake Ave Extension.Farley Santos, economic and community development advisor to Mayor Roberto Alves, said Mill Plain Road continues to be a major engine of economic growth for Danbury. He described the warehouse investment as another vote of confidence in the city’s economy.A new chapter for an old siteThe project will preserve the warehouse’s industrial role while adding modern office space and improving the surrounding property. That approach reflects a broader trend in which established commercial sites are updated rather than abandoned or completely rebuilt.For Danbury, the transaction brings together two local stories. A building associated with one family for generations is passing into the hands of another family with deep ties to the city, but with plans to modernise it and keep it active.With the purchase complete and renovation plans approved, the former Dandy Foods warehouse is set to become part of Mill Plain Road’s next phase of growth. The combined $8.5 million investment suggests confidence that older commercial properties can still play an important role in a changing local economy.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.title: A World War II pillbox in Dorset was transformed into a bat hibernation shelter in 2025; the concrete structure once formed part of Britain’s wartime defences
articles.summary: A World War II pillbox in Mudeford Wood, Christchurch, Dorset, had been converted into a shelter for protected bat species.
articles.body: A World War II pillbox in Mudeford Wood, Christchurch, Dorset, had been converted into a shelter for protected bat species. The concrete structure once served a military purpose, supporting defence and training ahead of operations such as the D-Day landings. In 2025, it was adapted to provide bats with a safe place to hibernate during winter.According to BCP Council, the project aims to support local bat populations while preserving an important part of the area's wartime history. The work also addresses anti-social behaviour and vandalism that threatened the structure. The former military shelter serves a new purpose, helping protect local wildlife while retaining its place in Christchurch's history.How a World War II pillbox in Mudeford Wood became a bat shelterThe pillbox stands in Mudeford Wood, a designated Site of Nature Conservation Interest (SNCI) known for its rich biodiversity. The site was formerly RAF Christchurch airfield, where aircraft production and military exercises took place during World War II.Two concrete pillboxes remain at the site as part of the airfield's wartime defences. One had become a target for vandalism and anti-social behaviour, putting its historical value and potential as a wildlife habitat at risk. After similar pillbox conversions in Suffolk and Studland, BCP Council decided to adapt the structure for bats. The completed project had given the former military shelter a new purpose, providing a potential refuge for local bat populations.The changes made to turn the pillbox into a bat shelterBCP Council's conservation team worked with Dorset bat ecologist Colin Morris to adapt the pillbox into a suitable hibernation shelter. A hibernaculum provides a secure chamber with stable temperatures and moist humidity, allowing bats to roost during hibernation while reducing the risk of interference from other mammals.The work included sealing the pillbox windows and installing a galvanised grille at the entrance. The grille allows bats to fly in and out freely while helping protect them from disturbance. These changes were designed to make the concrete structure suitable for use as a winter shelter. The project focuses on creating a secure environment for bats during an important period of their annual life cycle.Funding and new features highlight the pillbox's new purposeThe project was funded entirely through Heathland Mitigation Funding, made up of fees paid to the council by developers building new homes within a certain distance of protected heathlands. The funding supported the conversion of the pillbox into a wildlife shelter. To highlight the project and explain its purpose to residents, a commemorative sculpture had been installed at the site.New signage was also planned to inform visitors about the conservation work and the importance of bats to the ecosystem. Councillor Andy Hadley, Portfolio Holder for Climate Response, Environment and Energy, described the work as an innovative project that gives an important piece of local heritage a new purpose.Why the new shelter matters for bats in Mudeford WoodMudeford Wood supports several protected bat species, including Common Pipistrelle, Brown Long eared and Serotine bats. The new hibernaculum is intended to provide these local populations with a safe place to shelter during winter. Colin Morris said, “Protecting important sites like this, although small in stature are vital to the local population of bats and ‘once the word gets around in the batty world’ it's likely to become a regular, long-term, safe and secure haven for them during the important hibernation period. Hibernation sites are never as interesting as the summer, nursery sites and often overlooked, but without them, bats would struggle to survive.”You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.title: Airbnb hosts can no longer make guests strip beds and wash dishes under new rules
articles.summary: The updated policy will apply to all reservations booked on the accommodation site on or after 20 November.
articles.body:
Airbnb has changed its rules to limit what property hosts may ask guests to do - including when it comes to cleaning.

The updated guidelines state that hosts can now set seven standard house rules and can also add other "reasonable" requests.

Airbnb states that guests - who are required to pay a cleaning fee - should not be asked to complete tasks normally done by a cleaner, including washing dishes and stripping beds.

The new rules will apply to all reservations booked on or after 20 November on the accommodation marketplace.

"House rules help guests understand what hosts expect, but we've heard from our community that they can be confusing, onerous and hard to manage," Airbnb told the BBC.

"So, we've redesigned them to make them easier to discover and clearer to set, alongside a new policy that keeps requests reasonable, with no surprises."

According to the new requirements on the Airbnb website, hosts are generally not allowed to ask guests to complete tasks that "require significant effort or time, or would typically be performed by a cleaner, including stripping the bed, taking trash offsite, or washing and putting away dishes".

The company said it may grant exceptions in some circumstances. For example, guests can be asked to limit shower time if there are local drought-related water restrictions.

A property's rules will be displayed to guests more prominently moving forward and will appear in the guests' reservation reminders.

Contracts will only be allowed in limited circumstances, including when required by law or homeowners association rules.

While a host will not be able to impose fines, they remain in control of their house rules and requests, the company said.

If a host's request does not follow Airbnb policies, the issue will be flagged and the owner can appeal if they disagree.

Guests have for years complained about unreasonable tasks they we required to complete before departure, especially as they are required to pay cleaning fees.

TikTok videos from Airbnb hosts Cassie and Jon that show them closely inspecting their rental property in the US state of Georgia after guests leave have gone viral recently for their attention to detail.

One video from the couple, for example, accuses guests of "disrespecting the house rules" for leaving a television remote out of place.

They have been criticised for their strict rules and high standards but said in response that their content had been misinterpreted

Their videos have inspired other content creators to parody stringent hosts.

articles.title: Diabetes and ADHD drugs to be tested on Alzheimer's patients in new study
articles.summary: Drugs will be tested simultaneously, which it's hoped will speed up the process of finding new treatments for this common type of dementia.
articles.body:
A clinical trial has been launched in the UK which scientists hope could cut years from the search for new treatments for Alzheimer's disease.

It will test multiple drugs simultaneously, starting with two repurposed medicines already used to treat type 2 diabetes and attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD).

The study will examine whether the drugs can lessen symptoms such as memory and thinking problems, and help people maintain their quality of life.

Angela Bucksey, 67, from Cambridgeshire, was diagnosed with Alzheimer's in January and is the first person to begin treatment on the trial, called AD-SMART.

"We have Alzheimer's in the family," she told the BBC.

"My mother had it and my aunts, so it was a disappointment rather than a shock when I was diagnosed because I knew it would restrict my life.

"But I was determined that it wasn't going to define me."

Angela said she felt empowered joining the trial because "at least you are doing something".

"Instead of just sitting there, you're standing up and saying, I will fight back."

Alzheimer's is the most common type of dementia, affecting around 600,000 people in the UK.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham, whose father died from Alzheimer's last month, said he knew how it felt to lose a loved one to dementia, and had seen first-hand the devastating impact of the disease on families.

"That's why I'm proud to see this trial being launched in the UK, so that cutting-edge treatments can reach patients here as soon as possible," he said.

The AD-SMART study is what's known as a multi-arm, multi-stage platform trial where several treatments are tested simultaneously, with the results compared with one group of participants taking a placebo or dummy.

This means those involved have a higher likelihood of getting an active treatment than in a traditional trial.

If any drug isn't showing benefit it can be dropped quickly and a new treatment added in its place - the approach has been used successfully in cancer and motor neurone disease.

The two initial drugs being tested are metformin, used to treat type 2 diabetes, and atomoxetine, for ADHD, which were selected by an international panel of experts.

Both drugs may help reduce brain inflammation, which is a driver of neurodegeneration, said chief investigator Prof Paresh Malhotra, group leader at the UK Dementia Research Institute Centre for Care Research & Technology at Imperial College London.

"For too long, Alzheimer's research has moved at the pace of one drug, one trial, one answer - sometimes taking a decade or more before we know if we've found something that works," he told the BBC.

"We are applying advances from cancer and other conditions to accelerate testing of treatments for people with Alzheimer's disease."

For the drugs to be successful, the study has to show that they have beneficial effects on thinking and the ability to carry out everyday activities.

"That's what patients and their carers care about," said Prof Malhotra.

Some 1,200 participants with mild to moderate Alzheimer's will be recruited at more than 30 sites across the UK. Sites in Cambridgeshire, Surrey, London, Southampton and Edinburgh are already open.

Scientists expect to finish evaluating the first drugs in 2030 and, in that time, additional treatments are likely to be added.

All the participants will have regular health checks including cognitive tests, which will help researchers assess how effective the treatments are.

Angela Bucksey's husband Steve, who is her study partner, told the BBC: "Joining the trial has brought us back from the despair of a diagnosis which everybody recognises is non-recoverable.

"People who know we are on a drug trial understand that we're doing something about it and, rather than be sorry for us, they can be encouraging."

Dr Sheona Scales, director of research at Alzheimer's Research UK said "time is precious" for people living with Alzheimer's disease and more treatment options are urgently needed.

People with a confirmed Alzheimer's diagnosis who would like to take part can register their interest on the AD-SMART website .

The trial is being led by the UK Dementia Research Institute and Alzheimer's Research UK.

Partners include the National Institute for Health and Care Research, the Medical Research Council and Health Data Research UK, with funding by UK government.

articles.title: UK City of Culture: Blackpool, Milton Keynes, Sheffield and Wrexham shortlisted for 2029
articles.summary: The winner, announced in early 2027, will receive £10m to deliver a year of cultural activities.
articles.body:
Blackpool, Milton Keynes, Sheffield and Wrexham have been shortlisted to become the UK's City of Culture in 2029.

The winning location will be announced in May and will be the fifth holder of the title - following Derry-Londonderry, Hull, Coventry and Bradford.

A different location is given the City of Culture title every four years. Each shortlisted city will now receive at least £125,000 from the government to do further work on their bid.

The eventual winner will receive £10m to deliver a year of cultural events and activities drawing on its "local strengths and stories".

Culture Secretary Lisa Nandy said the shortlisted cities "have shown the pride that exists in their places with the incredible culture on their doorsteps".

Three of the contenders are in England and one in Wales. They were chosen from a longlist of nine, which also included Inverness, Ipswich, Middlesbrough, Portsmouth and Swindon.

What is it known for? Its landmark Blackpool Tower, Pleasure Beach and Illuminations. It also hosts a major dance festival and an annual visit from Strictly Come Dancing. The Showtown museum celebrates Blackpool's history as a showbiz and comedy hotspot.

What have they said? Lynn Williams, leader of Blackpool Council, said: "Blackpool has been entertaining people for generations, and now we have the chance to show the country exactly what our town is made of."

She added: "Blackpool has never been a town that stands still. It is proud, working-class culture that has always been about bringing people together, having fun and making something happen."

What is it known for? Constructed in the 1960s and 70s, Milton Keynes is known for its US-style grid road system and numerous roundabouts. It is home to historic World War II codebreaking centre Bletchley Park, now a museum, and the National Bowl, an amphitheatre that has hosted concerts by Oasis, Queen and David Bowie.

What have they said? Milton Keynes' bid described it as "a city built on imagination – a place where innovation, diversity and creativity thrive side by side".

Councillor Jane Carr, leader of Milton Keynes City Council, said: "We're now on the cusp of the 60th anniversary of our founding and have so much to look forward to during this landmark year and beyond."

What is it known for? The traditional centre of steel and cutlery manufacturing, Sheffield has since become known for musical exports like the Arctic Monkeys and Pulp, for its annual documentary film festival, and for the Crucible - one of the leading theatres outside London.

What have they said? The city's bid put its spotlight on Sheffield's "world-renowned creative heritage, as well as our ambitious future plans".

Celebrating its place on the shortlist, councillor Fran Belbin, leader of the city council, said: "Sheffield is a city built on creativity, innovation and community spirit... Culture is part of who we are."

What is it known for? North Wales's largest city was a powerhouse of the industrial revolution, and most recently hit the headlines when its historic football club Wrexham AFC was bought by Hollywood actors Ryan Reynolds and Rob McElhenney.

What have they said? The bid said: "Our ambition is simple but bold: to make Wrexham the world's most playful place."

Joanna Knight OBE, chair of the Wrexham bid, styled as Wrecsam2029, explained: "There's a real sense that something very special is happening here. Just imagine what becoming the first Welsh UK City of Culture could mean... the opportunities are enormous."

articles.title: The graduates ditching the UK to work abroad
articles.summary: With graduate jobs hard to come by, more young adults are reported to be considering emigrating.
articles.body:
Last year Rachel James quit her corporate job in London, packed a suitcase and booked a one-way ticket to Sydney, without a job lined up or a plan in place.

"I went for a fresh start," says the 26-year-old from Surrey. "To take a risk and try something completely different. With the worst case being there will always be a flight home if all fails."

More than one in 10 UK university students are now planning to move abroad for better opportunities after they have graduated, up from 7.8% two years ago, according to a survey of 15,000 final year university students.

Meanwhile, a study by the Institute of Student Employers (ISE) says that competition for graduate jobs in the UK was at a three-decade high.

UK employers now receive 140 applications per graduate vacancy on average, an increase of 14% from 2025, and up from just 30 applications per vacancy 20 years ago, according to the ISE's report .

For young British adults going abroad, where are they heading?

Australia: 'The weather's beautiful, even in the winter'

While there is no age-specific data for which countries people go to, Australia remains by far the most popular nation for British adults overall who move abroad, official figures show.

In addition to Australia's weather and use of the English language, another reason is its visa-friendly policy. Under its Working Holiday Maker programme, British passport holders between the ages of 18 and 35 can live in Australia for up to three years.

Rachel, who graduated from Loughborough University in 2022 with a degree in English, had been working for insurance giant PricewaterhouseCoopers in the UK. She now has a job in marketing in Sydney for gym chain Fitness First.

She says her annual salary has gone down from £42,000 to £37,000, while she now pays $AUS 2,000 (£1,000) a month to rent a two-bedroom apartment with a friend, similar to what she was paying in London.

Despite having less disposable income, she has no regrets. "The weather's beautiful, even in the winter, and the walks on my doorstep are unmatched.

"People want to leave work at 5pm so they can go and do their hobbies - whether it's surfing, running, enjoying the sunset, a picnic or sunset yoga. I didn't come with career progression as a focus - it's more about the different way of life."

Around two-thirds of British nationals who emigrate are aged between 16 and 34, according to the most recent figures from the UK's Office for National Statistics.

It said that 75,000 more people in that age bracket left the UK in 2025 than arrived.

After Australia the next most popular destination for British adults is the US.

Charlie West, 25, from Cheshire, moved to the States in 2024 for better pay and opportunities in academia after he completed a masters in medieval studies at Oxford University.

West is now two years in to a six-year funded PhD course at Yale's Department of Italian Studies, which includes him teaching.

"I really wanted to do a PhD but it's difficult to get funding in the UK, particularly in the humanities, and funded stipends are about £21,000. I'd have had to work [outside academia] at the same time to afford to live.

"In the US I'm paid $51,000 a year (£37,770), about to rise to $52,000, and it comes with a lot more opportunities to teach and travel to conferences."

Europe: 'If you can work across the EU there are more opportunities'

The European Union also remains popular with young Britons looking to move abroad, although the visa requirements since Brexit have made it more difficult.

One way to get into the European jobs market is to have studied in the EU. International graduates can apply for a permanent residence permit after their degree ends.

This is what Owein Iveson, 24, from Sunderland, is doing as he is about to graduate from Finland's Aalto University with a masters in design.

Owein says he "fell in love with the country" after visiting for the first time in 2020.

"Finland's a beautiful country," he says. "The streets are very clean. It's a very quiet lifestyle. The nature is fantastic and the public transport works really efficiently."

Owein lives in Espoo, a city about 15 minutes on the metro from Helsinki, and doesn't expect to return to the UK anytime soon.

"To be honest the jobs market is not great in Finland, but there is high demand for IT workers, and if you can work across the EU there are many more opportunities."

Immigration lawyer John Kiely, a London-based partner at international law firm Howard Kennedy, says it is easy to see why more UK graduates are looking overseas.

"When you combine student debt, high housing costs, relatively weak wage growth and uncertainty about future employment, the willingness to roll the dice somewhere else becomes quite rational."

Back in Sydney, Rachel says the city simply offers a better quality of life than London.

"I don't see life in Sydney as any more expensive than if I was in London, but personally I have found the perks in Sydney better."
